CHAPTER XV. A STRANGE HOSTESS

I travelled on attended by the moon. As usual she was full--I had never
seen her other--and to-night as she sank I thought I perceived something
like a smile on her countenance.

When her under edge was a little below the horizon, there appeared in
the middle of her disc, as if it had been painted upon it, a cottage,
through the open door and window of which she shone; and with the sight
came the conviction that I was expected there. Almost immediately the
moon was gone, and the cottage had vanished; the night was rapidly
growing dark, and my way being across a close succession of small
ravines, I resolved to remain where I was and expect the morning. I
stretched myself, therefore, in a sandy hollow, made my supper off the
fruits the children had given me at parting, and was soon asleep.

I woke suddenly, saw above me constellations unknown to my former world,
and had lain for a while gazing at them, when I became aware of a figure
seated on the ground a little way from and above me. I was startled, as
one is on discovering all at once that he is not alone. The figure was
between me and the sky, so that I saw its outline well. From where I lay
low in the hollow, it seemed larger than human.

It moved its head, and then first I saw that its back was toward me.

“Will you not come with me?” said a sweet, mellow voice, unmistakably a
woman’s.

Wishing to learn more of my hostess,

“I thank you,” I replied, “but I am not uncomfortable here. Where would
you have me go? I like sleeping in the open air.”

“There is no hurt in the air,” she returned; “but the creatures that
roam the night in these parts are not such as a man would willingly have
about him while he sleeps.”

“I have not been disturbed,” I said.

“No; I have been sitting by you ever since you lay down.”

“That is very kind of you! How came you to know I was here? Why do you
show me such favour?”

“I saw you,” she answered, still with her back to me, “in the light of
the moon, just as she went down. I see badly in the day, but at night
perfectly. The shadow of my house would have hidden you, but both
its doors were open. I was out on the waste, and saw you go into this
hollow. You were asleep, however, before I could reach you, and I was
not willing to disturb you. People are frightened if I come on them
suddenly. They call me the Cat-woman. It is not my name.”

I remembered what the children had told me--that she was very ugly, and
scratched. But her voice was gentle, and its tone a little apologetic:
she could not be a bad giantess!

“You shall not hear it from me,” I answered, “Please tell me what I MAY
call you!”

“When you know me, call me by the name that seems to you to fit me,” she
replied: “that will tell me what sort you are. People do not often give
me the right one. It is well when they do.”

“I suppose, madam, you live in the cottage I saw in the heart of the
moon?”

“I do. I live there alone, except when I have visitors. It is a poor
place, but I do what I can for my guests, and sometimes their sleep is
sweet to them.”

Her voice entered into me, and made me feel strangely still.

“I will go with you, madam,” I said, rising.

She rose at once, and without a glance behind her led the way. I could
see her just well enough to follow. She was taller than myself, but not
so tall as I had thought her. That she never turned her face to me made
me curious--nowise apprehensive, her voice rang so true. But how was I
to fit her with a name who could not see her? I strove to get alongside
of her, but failed: when I quickened my pace she quickened hers, and
kept easily ahead of me. At length I did begin to grow a little afraid.
Why was she so careful not to be seen? Extraordinary ugliness would
account for it: she might fear terrifying me! Horror of an inconceivable
monstrosity began to assail me: was I following through the dark
an unheard of hideousness? Almost I repented of having accepted her
hospitality.

Neither spoke, and the silence grew unbearable. I MUST break it!

“I want to find my way,” I said, “to a place I have heard of, but whose
name I have not yet learned. Perhaps you can tell it me!”

“Describe it, then, and I will direct you. The stupid Bags know nothing,
and the careless little Lovers forget almost everything.”

“Where do those live?”

“You are just come from them!”

“I never heard those names before!”

“You would not hear them. Neither people knows its own name!”

“Strange!”

“Perhaps so! but hardly any one anywhere knows his own name! It would
make many a fine gentleman stare to hear himself addressed by what is
really his name!”

I held my peace, beginning to wonder what my name might be.

“What now do you fancy yours?” she went on, as if aware of my thought.
“But, pardon me, it is a matter of no consequence.”

I had actually opened my mouth to answer her, when I discovered that my
name was gone from me. I could not even recall the first letter of it!
This was the second time I had been asked my name and could not tell it!

“Never mind,” she said; “it is not wanted. Your real name, indeed, is
written on your forehead, but at present it whirls about so irregularly
that nobody can read it. I will do my part to steady it. Soon it will go
slower, and, I hope, settle at last.”

This startled me, and I was silent.

We had left the channels and walked a long time, but no sign of the
cottage yet appeared.

“The Little Ones told me,” I said at length, “of a smooth green country,
pleasant to the feet!”

“Yes?” she returned.

“They told me too of a girl giantess that was queen somewhere: is that
her country?”

“There is a city in that grassy land,” she replied, “where a woman is
princess. The city is called Bulika. But certainly the princess is not
a girl! She is older than this world, and came to it from yours--with
a terrible history, which is not over yet. She is an evil person, and
prevails much with the Prince of the Power of the Air. The people of
Bulika were formerly simple folk, tilling the ground and pasturing
sheep. She came among them, and they received her hospitably. She taught
them to dig for diamonds and opals and sell them to strangers, and made
them give up tillage and pasturage and build a city. One day they found
a huge snake and killed it; which so enraged her that she declared
herself their princess, and became terrible to them. The name of the
country at that time was THE LAND OF WATERS; for the dry channels,
of which you have crossed so many, were then overflowing with live
torrents; and the valley, where now the Bags and the Lovers have their
fruit-trees, was a lake that received a great part of them. But the
wicked princess gathered up in her lap what she could of the water over
the whole country, closed it in an egg, and carried it away. Her lap,
however, would not hold more than half of it; and the instant she was
gone, what she had not yet taken fled away underground, leaving the
country as dry and dusty as her own heart. Were it not for the waters
under it, every living thing would long ago have perished from it. For
where no water is, no rain falls; and where no rain falls, no springs
rise. Ever since then, the princess has lived in Bulika, holding the
inhabitants in constant terror, and doing what she can to keep them from
multiplying. Yet they boast and believe themselves a prosperous, and
certainly are a self-satisfied people--good at bargaining and buying,
good at selling and cheating; holding well together for a common
interest, and utterly treacherous where interests clash; proud of their
princess and her power, and despising every one they get the better of;
never doubting themselves the most honourable of all the nations, and
each man counting himself better than any other. The depth of their
worthlessness and height of their vainglory no one can understand who
has not been there to see, who has not learned to know the miserable
misgoverned and self-deceived creatures.”

“I thank you, madam. And now, if you please, will you tell me something
about the Little Ones--the Lovers? I long heartily to serve them. Who
and what are they? and how do they come to be there? Those children are
the greatest wonder I have found in this world of wonders.”

“In Bulika you may, perhaps, get some light on those matters. There is
an ancient poem in the library of the palace, I am told, which of course
no one there can read, but in which it is plainly written that after the
Lovers have gone through great troubles and learned their own name, they
will fill the land, and make the giants their slaves.”

“By that time they will have grown a little, will they not?” I said.

“Yes, they will have grown; yet I think too they will not have grown.
It is possible to grow and not to grow, to grow less and to grow bigger,
both at once--yes, even to grow by means of not growing!”

“Your words are strange, madam!” I rejoined. “But I have heard it said
that some words, because they mean more, appear to mean less!”

“That is true, and such words HAVE to be understood. It were well for
the princess of Bulika if she heard what the very silence of the land
is shouting in her ears all day long! But she is far too clever to
understand anything.”

“Then I suppose, when the little Lovers are grown, their land will have
water again?”

“Not exactly so: when they are thirsty enough, they will have water,
and when they have water, they will grow. To grow, they must have water.
And, beneath, it is flowing still.”

“I have heard that water twice,” I said; “--once when I lay down to wait
for the moon--and when I woke the sun was shining! and once when I
fell, all but killed by the bad giant. Both times came the voices of the
water, and healed me.”

The woman never turned her head, and kept always a little before me, but
I could hear every word that left her lips, and her voice much reminded
me of the woman’s in the house of death. Much of what she said, I did
not understand, and therefore cannot remember. But I forgot that I had
ever been afraid of her.

We went on and on, and crossed yet a wide tract of sand before reaching
the cottage. Its foundation stood in deep sand, but I could see that
it was a rock. In character the cottage resembled the sexton’s, but had
thicker walls. The door, which was heavy and strong, opened immediately
into a large bare room, which had two little windows opposite each
other, without glass. My hostess walked in at the open door out of which
the moon had looked, and going straight to the farthest corner, took a
long white cloth from the floor, and wound it about her head and face.
Then she closed the other door, in at which the moon had looked, trimmed
a small horn lantern that stood on the hearth, and turned to receive me.

“You are very welcome, Mr. Vane!” she said, calling me by the name I had
forgotten. “Your entertainment will be scanty, but, as the night is not
far spent, and the day not at hand, it is better you should be indoors.
Here you will be safe, and a little lack is not a great misery.”

“I thank you heartily, madam,” I replied. “But, seeing you know the name
I could not tell you, may I not now know yours?”

“My name is Mara,” she answered.

Then I remembered the sexton and the little black cat.

“Some people,” she went on, “take me for Lot’s wife, lamenting over
Sodom; and some think I am Rachel, weeping for her children; but I am
neither of those.”

“I thank you again, Mara,” I said. “--May I lie here on your floor till
the morning?”

“At the top of that stair,” she answered, “you will find a bed--on which
some have slept better than they expected, and some have waked all the
night and slept all the next day. It is not a very soft one, but it is
better than the sand--and there are no hyenas sniffing about it!”

The stair, narrow and steep, led straight up from the room to an
unceiled and unpartitioned garret, with one wide, low dormer window.
Close under the sloping roof stood a narrow bed, the sight of which with
its white coverlet made me shiver, so vividly it recalled the couches in
the chamber of death. On the table was a dry loaf, and beside it a cup
of cold water. To me, who had tasted nothing but fruit for months, they
were a feast.

“I must leave you in the dark,” my hostess called from the bottom of the
stair. “This lantern is all the light I have, and there are things to do
to-night.”

“It is of no consequence, thank you, madam,” I returned. “To eat and
drink, to lie down and sleep, are things that can be done in the dark.”

“Rest in peace,” she said.

I ate up the loaf, drank the water every drop, and laid myself down.
The bed was hard, the covering thin and scanty, and the night cold: I
dreamed that I lay in the chamber of death, between the warrior and the
lady with the healing wound.

I woke in the middle of the night, thinking I heard low noises of wild
animals.

“Creatures of the desert scenting after me, I suppose!” I said to
myself, and, knowing I was safe, would have gone to sleep again. But
that instant a rough purring rose to a howl under my window, and I
sprang from my bed to see what sort of beast uttered it.

Before the door of the cottage, in the full radiance of the moon, a tall
woman stood, clothed in white, with her back toward me. She was stooping
over a large white animal like a panther, patting and stroking it with
one hand, while with the other she pointed to the moon half-way up the
heaven, then drew a perpendicular line to the horizon. Instantly the
creature darted off with amazing swiftness in the direction indicated.
For a moment my eyes followed it, then sought the woman; but she was
gone, and not yet had I seen her face! Again I looked after the animal,
but whether I saw or only fancied a white speck in the distance, I could
not tell.--What did it mean? What was the monster-cat sent off to do? I
shuddered, and went back to my bed. Then I remembered that, when I lay
down in the sandy hollow outside, the moon was setting; yet here
she was, a few hours after, shining in all her glory! “Everything is
uncertain here,” I said to myself, “--even the motions of the heavenly
bodies!”

I learned afterward that there were several moons in the service of this
world, but the laws that ruled their times and different orbits I failed
to discover.

Again I fell asleep, and slept undisturbed.

When I went down in the morning, I found bread and water waiting me, the
loaf so large that I ate only half of it. My hostess sat muffled beside
me while I broke my fast, and except to greet me when I entered, never
opened her mouth until I asked her to instruct me how to arrive at
Bulika. She then told me to go up the bank of the river-bed until it
disappeared; then verge to the right until I came to a forest--in which
I might spend a night, but which I must leave with my face to the rising
moon. Keeping in the same direction, she said, until I reached a running
stream, I must cross that at right angles, and go straight on until I
saw the city on the horizon.

I thanked her, and ventured the remark that, looking out of the window
in the night, I was astonished to see her messenger understand her so
well, and go so straight and so fast in the direction she had indicated.

“If I had but that animal of yours to guide me--” I went on, hoping to
learn something of its mission, but she interrupted me, saying,

“It was to Bulika she went--the shortest way.”

“How wonderfully intelligent she looked!”

“Astarte knows her work well enough to be sent to do it,” she answered.

“Have you many messengers like her?”

“As many as I require.”

“Are they hard to teach?”

“They need no teaching. They are all of a certain breed, but not one of
the breed is like another. Their origin is so natural it would seem to
you incredible.”

“May I not know it?”

“A new one came to me last night--from your head while you slept.”

I laughed.

“All in this world seem to love mystery!” I said to myself. “Some chance
word of mine suggested an idea--and in this form she embodies the small
fact!”

“Then the creature is mine!” I cried.

“Not at all!” she answered. “That only can be ours in whose existence
our will is a factor.”

“Ha! a metaphysician too!” I remarked inside, and was silent.

“May I take what is left of the loaf?” I asked presently.

“You will want no more to-day,” she replied.

“To-morrow I may!” I rejoined.

She rose and went to the door, saying as she went,

“It has nothing to do with to-morrow--but you may take it if you will.”

She opened the door, and stood holding it. I rose, taking up the
bread--but lingered, much desiring to see her face.

“Must I go, then?” I asked.

“No one sleeps in my house two nights together!” she answered.

“I thank you, then, for your hospitality, and bid you farewell!” I said,
and turned to go.

“The time will come when you must house with me many days and many
nights,” she murmured sadly through her muffling.

“Willingly,” I replied.

“Nay, NOT willingly!” she answered.

I said to myself that she was right--I would not willingly be her guest
a second time! but immediately my heart rebuked me, and I had scarce
crossed the threshold when I turned again.

She stood in the middle of the room; her white garments lay like foamy
waves at her feet, and among them the swathings of her face: it was
lovely as a night of stars. Her great gray eyes looked up to heaven;
tears were flowing down her pale cheeks. She reminded me not a little
of the sexton’s wife, although the one looked as if she had not wept for
thousands of years, and the other as if she wept constantly behind the
wrappings of her beautiful head. Yet something in the very eyes that
wept seemed to say, “Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in
the morning.”

I had bowed my head for a moment, about to kneel and beg her
forgiveness, when, looking up in the act, I found myself outside a
doorless house. I went round and round it, but could find no entrance.

I had stopped under one of the windows, on the point of calling aloud my
repentant confession, when a sudden wailing, howling scream invaded my
ears, and my heart stood still. Something sprang from the window above
my head, and lighted beyond me. I turned, and saw a large gray cat, its
hair on end, shooting toward the river-bed. I fell with my face in the
sand, and seemed to hear within the house the gentle sobbing of one who
suffered but did not repent.

I traveled on with the moon as my constant companion. She hung full, as she always did – I had never once seen her crescent or dark in this strange land – and on that night, as she sank low toward the horizon, I could have sworn I caught a soft, secret smile tugging at the edges of her craters. When her lower rim dipped just below the line of the sands, a cottage bloomed clear in the very center of her glowing disc, painted as if by brushstroke against her silver: door and windows stood wide, and her own light poured straight through them. The certainty hit me like a soft hand on my shoulder: I was expected there.

In the next breath the moon winked out, and the cottage vanished with her. The dark came on fast, and the road ahead snaked through a jagged chain of small, shadow-choked ravines. I decided to make camp right where I stood. I stretched out in a soft sandy hollow, supped on the leftover fruit the little Lovers had pressed on me at parting, and fell asleep almost instantly.

I woke abruptly. New constellations blazed overhead, patterns no Earth astronomer had ever mapped, and I lay staring up at them for long minutes before I noticed the figure seated on the rise of ground a little way above me. The shock of realizing I was not alone pricked at my skin. The silhouette was backlit against the alien sky, looming larger than any human ought to be from my vantage low in the hollow. It turned its head, and I saw its back was fully turned to me.

“Will you not come with me?” The voice was sweet, mellow, unmistakably a woman’s.

“Thank you,” I called back, not wanting to seem rude, “but I’m quite comfortable here. Where do you mean to take me? I’ve always liked sleeping under open sky.”

“There is no harm in the air,” she replied. “But the night creatures that roam these wastes are not the sort a man would choose to have sniffing at his blankets while he sleeps.”

“I haven’t been disturbed yet,” I said.

“No. I’ve sat beside you ever since you laid down.”

That took me aback. “That is very kind of you. How did you find me? Why do me such a favour?”

“I saw you,” she answered, still not turning to show me her face, “in the last sliver of the moon’s light before she set. I see very poorly in the day, but perfectly at night. The shadow of my cottage would have hidden you from view, but both its doors were standing wide. I was out wandering the waste, and watched you slip down into this hollow. I did not want to wake you – people get frightened when I creep up on them unannounced. They call me the Cat-woman. It is not my name.”

I remembered the children’s warnings: that she was hideously ugly, that she scratched strangers who crossed her. But her voice was gentle, almost apologetic, and I could not bring myself to fear her. “I will not call you that,” I said. “Please tell me what I ought to call you.”

“When you know me well enough, give me the name that feels like it fits,” she said. “That will tell me what kind of man you are. People rarely give me the right one. It is a good day when they do.”

“Then I suppose you live in that cottage I saw, glowing right in the heart of the moon?”

“I do. I live there alone, save for the guests that find their way to me. It is a humble little place, but I do what I can for them. Sometimes their sleep there is sweeter than any they have known elsewhere.”

Her voice seeped into my bones, and I felt an unexpected stillness settle over me. I climbed to my feet. “I will come with you, madam.”

She rose at once, and led the way without a single glance over her shoulder. I could just make out her outline well enough to follow. She was taller than me, but not nearly as giant as she had looked at first from the hollow. That she refused to turn to face me sparked my curiosity, not fear – her voice rang too true for me to doubt her. But how could I ever find a name that fit a woman I could not see? I tried to match her stride, to slip beside her, but no matter how fast I stepped, she matched my pace and kept a steady easy lead a few feet ahead. After a while a faint prickle of unease crept in. Why was she so determined not to be seen? Extreme ugliness would explain it – she might fear terrifying me. A sudden, cold horror of some inconceivable monstrosity snaked through my chest: was I trailing some unnameable abomination through the dark? I almost regretted agreeing to follow her. The silence stretched too long, thick and unbearable, so I broke it.

“I am trying to find a place I have heard of, but do not know its name,” I said. “Perhaps you can point me the way?”

“Describe it, and I will guide you. The stupid Bags know nothing of such things, and the careless little Lovers forget almost everything.”

“Where do those two peoples live?”

“You just came from their lands,” she said.

“I never heard those names before.”

“Of course you did not. Neither people knows its own true name.”

“How strange,” I said.

“Perhaps. But hardly anyone anywhere knows their own real name. Many a fine proud gentleman would stare in shock if someone called him by the name that actually belongs to him.”

I fell quiet, wondering what my own true name might be.

“You are thinking of yours right now, aren’t you?” she said, as if she could read my thoughts. “But never mind it. It is of no consequence. Your real name is written on your forehead, but right now it whirls around too fast for anyone to read. I will help it steady. Soon it will slow, and settle, I hope, at last.”

That startled me, and I said no more. We had left the ravines far behind, but there was still no sign of her cottage. “The Little Ones – the Lovers – told me of a smooth green country, soft underfoot,” I said.

“Yes?”

“They spoke too of a girl giantess who is queen there somewhere. Is that her land?”

“There is a city in that grassy realm,” she said, “ruled by a woman they call their princess. The city is named Bulika. But she is no girl. She is older than this world, and came here from yours, with a terrible history that has not yet run its course. She is evil, and holds great favour with the Prince of the Power of the Air. The people of Bulika were once simple folk, tilling the soil and pasturing sheep. They welcomed her when she arrived, and she rewarded their kindness by teaching them to dig for diamonds and opals to sell to strangers. She made them abandon their fields and their flocks, and build that city of stone. One day they found a great serpent and killed it, and that drove her to rage. She declared herself their princess, and became a terror to them. Back then, this whole region was called The Land of Waters. All those dry, empty river beds you have crossed were once full of rushing, living torrents, and the valley where the Lovers’ fruit trees grow was a great lake that fed them. But the wicked princess gathered half the waters of the whole land into her lap, sealed them up inside a hollow egg, and carried it away. The rest of the water fled straight underground the moment she was gone, leaving the country as dry and dusty as her own heart. If not for the hidden waters still flowing beneath the sand, every living thing here would have perished long ago. Where there is no surface water, no rain ever falls, and where no rain falls, no springs rise. Ever since, she has ruled Bulika, holding her people in constant fear, doing all she can to stop them from growing in number. And yet they boast of their prosperity, think themselves so very self-satisfied. They are good at bargaining, good at cheating, they stick close together when their interests align, and will betray each other without a second thought the moment those interests clash. They are proud of their cruel princess, and despise everyone they can outwit. They have not the faintest doubt that they are the most honourable nation alive, and each man among them thinks he is better than every other. No one who has not walked their streets can understand how deep their worthlessness runs, how high their vainglory towers.”

“Thank you for telling me,” I said. “Now tell me of the Little Ones, the Lovers. I want more than anything to help them. They are the greatest wonder I have found in this world of wonders.”

“Perhaps you will find answers to that in Bulika. There is an ancient poem locked in the palace library, no one alive there can read it anymore, but it says clearly that after the Lovers pass through great trials and learn their own true name, they will fill the land, and make the giants their slaves.”

“By that time they will have grown a little, I suppose?” I said.

“They will have grown. And yet, I think they will also not have grown. It is possible to grow and not grow at the same time, to grow smaller and bigger all at once – even to grow by means of not growing at all.”

“Your words are very strange, madam,” I said. “But I have heard it said that some words seem to mean less, because they actually hold far more meaning than we can grasp.”

“That is true. Those kinds of words have to be felt to be understood. It would serve the princess of Bulika well if she could hear what the very silence of this land is shouting in her ears all day long. But she is far too clever to ever understand anything that matters.”

“Then when the little Lovers are grown, the water will come back to the land?”

“Not exactly. When they are thirsty enough, they will find the water. And when they have water, they will begin to grow. To grow, they must have water. And deep beneath the sand, it is still flowing.”

“I heard that water twice before,” I said. “Once when I laid down to wait for the moon, and woke to sunlight, once when that cruel bad giant almost killed me. Both times the water’s voices came, and healed me.”

She never turned her head, never broke her steady pace a few feet ahead, but every word she spoke was clear as a bell, and her voice reminded me sharply of the soft healer woman I had met in the house of death. Much of what she said I could not parse, and so cannot now recall, but I had long since forgotten every last flicker of fear I had felt for her. We crossed a wide stretch of soft dune sand before the cottage finally came into view. It sat half sunk in the dunes, its foundations hewn out of solid rock. Its walls were thick, thicker than the old sexton’s cottage I had visited earlier, and its door stood open to us. We stepped straight into a large bare room, with two small, unglazed windows set opposite each other.

My hostess walked straight to the far corner, lifted a long white linen cloth from the floor, and wound it tight around her head and face, covering all her features. Then she shut the second door, trimmed a small horn lantern sitting on the hearth, and turned to face me.

“You are very welcome, Mr. Vane,” she said, calling me by the name I had realized I could not remember just a little while before. “Your entertainment will be scanty. The night is almost spent, but dawn is not yet here, and it is far safer for you to be inside these walls. A little lack of comfort is no great harm.”

“I thank you with all my heart, Mara,” I said, and the name came to my lips unbidden. At once I remembered the old sexton, and the little black cat he had kept by his hearth.

“Some people take me for Lot’s wife, still turned to salt and lamenting over Sodom,” she said. “Some think I am Rachel, weeping for her lost children. But I am neither of those.”

“Mara, may I lie here on your floor until morning?” I asked.

“Up that narrow stair you will find a bed,” she said. “Some who have slept there woke feeling lighter than they ever had, some lay awake all night and slept straight through the next full day. It is not soft, but it is far better than the sand – and there are no hyenas sniffing around its legs.”

The stair was steep and tight, leading straight up to an unceiled garret with one wide, low dormer window. A narrow bed stood under the sloped roof, its white linen coverlet sending a sharp shiver down my spine, so vividly it recalled the couches in that strange chamber of death. On the small table beside it sat a dry loaf and a cup of cold clear water. After months of eating nothing but wild fruit, it looked like a feast.

“I will leave you in the dark,” Mara called up from the bottom of the stair. “This lantern is the only light I have, and there are things I must tend to tonight.”

“It is no trouble at all, thank you,” I called back. “Eating, drinking, lying down and sleeping are all things one can do perfectly well in the dark.”

“Rest in peace,” she said.

I ate the whole loaf, drank every drop of the water, and laid down. The bed was hard, the covers thin, the night cold, and I dreamed I was back in the chamber of death, lying between the great fallen warrior and the lady with the healing wound. I woke deep in the night, hearing faint distant wild animal noises on the wind. “Desert creatures sniffing for me,” I told myself, and was about to roll over and fall back asleep when a rough, deep purr rose outside my window, climbing up into a full, thundering howl. I sprang from the bed to see what kind of beast made that sound.

Outside the cottage door, bathed in the full silver glow of the moon, stood Mara, tall and clad all in white, her back turned to me. She was kneeling, stroking a huge white panther-like creature that purred under her hands, one hand patting its head, the other pointing straight up to the moon hanging half-way up the sky, then drawing a straight line down to the distant horizon. The creature bolted off at impossible speed, straight in the direction she had pointed. I followed it with my eyes for a moment, then looked back for Mara – but she was gone. I had still never seen her face. When I looked for the great cat, I could not tell if the faint white speck far off on the sand was real, or just a trick of the moonlight. What did it mean? What mission had she sent that monstrous cat out to complete? I shuddered, and climbed back into bed. Then a thought hit me: the moon had been setting when I laid down in the sandy hollow, and now a few hours later it was halfway up the sky, full and bright. Everything in this world was unknowable, even the paths of the stars. I learned later this world had a whole host of moons, each bound to different rules, and no mortal could ever map their orbits.

I fell asleep again, and did not wake until full dawn. Downstairs, Mara had left more bread and water waiting for me. The loaf was so large I could only eat half of it. She sat across from me, still fully muffled in her white cloth, and did not speak until I asked her the way to Bulika. She told me to follow the high bank of the dry river bed until it vanished, then veer right until I reached a thick forest. I could spend one night there, but I had to leave the woods facing the rising moon. Keep that same path, she said, until I found a running stream of living water, cross it at a right angle, and walk straight on until the spires of Bulika rose over the horizon.

I thanked her, and mentioned that I had looked out my window in the night, and been astonished to see her great cat messenger understand her signs so perfectly, race off so fast. “If I had a creature like that to guide me,” I said, fishing for what she might tell me of its mission, but she cut me off.

“It is heading straight for Bulika. The shortest possible way.”

“It looked so intelligent.”

“Astarte knows her work well enough to be trusted with it,” she said.

“Do you have many messengers like her?”

“As many as I need.”

“Are they difficult to teach?”

“They need no teaching. They are all of one strange breed, but no two of them are ever the same. Their origin is so natural, you would think it impossible if I told you.”

“Will you tell me how they come to be?”

“A new one was born just last night,” she said. “Out of your own wandering thoughts, while you slept in the sand.”

I laughed. “Everyone in this world seems to love their mysteries,” I thought to myself. “Some stray thought of mine must have caught root, and she gave it that big cat form.”

“Then that creature is mine?” I said.

“Not at all,” she replied. “Nothing is truly yours unless your will helped make it exist.”

I smiled to myself, surprised. A metaphysician too, I thought. “May I take the rest of the loaf with me?” I asked.

“You will not need more food today,” she said.

“But I might need it tomorrow!”

She rose and walked to the door. “It has nothing to do with tomorrow – but take it if you wish.” She held the door open for me. I picked up the leftover bread, but lingered, burning with the desperate wish to see her face. “Must I go then?” I asked.

“No one sleeps in my house two nights in a row,” she said, her voice soft and muffled through the cloth.

“Thank you for your hospitality, farewell,” I said, turning to step across the threshold.

“The time will come when you will have to house with me for many days and many nights,” she murmured sadly.

“I will come willingly,” I said.

“No,” she said. “You will not come willingly.”

I thought to myself that she was right – I never would have chosen to return here a second time of my own free will. But then my heart rebuked me, and before I had fully crossed the line out of the cottage, I turned back.

She was standing in the middle of the room, the loose white linen of her outer clothes pooling at her feet like foaming ocean waves, and the cloth that had wrapped her face lay discarded among them. Her face was as beautiful as a night of unbroken starlight. Her great gray eyes were lifted up to the sky
